summary:
Manisa falls under Turkey's national legal and security framework. The sources behind this record contain no statute, incident, police action or court decision specific to Manisa province, so a trans visitor's exposure here is the national position as documented elsewhere in this map.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender recognition has been available since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised; marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a trans person who has legally changed the registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from the military.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' carry up to 3 years' imprisonment and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to 4 years; amend civil-code article 40 ('Changing Sex') to raise the gender-affirming care minimum age from 18 to 25 with mandatory infertility requirements and government-approved hospital evaluation; and imprison care providers up to 7 years and trans patients up to 3 years. This is national legislation. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

A February 2026 press report described legislation considering criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison; that provision was not included in the 2026 omnibus, the 12th judicial package. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

Authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches in June 2025; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Since 2015 authorities have banned pride events in most years, using tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions against those who defied the bans.

In June 2025 Turkey's health ministry medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21, despite existing law permitting access from 18. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association for sharing 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. In September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involved 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses.

In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49.
tangentialFactors:
The nearest named provincial action to Manisa is in İzmir, where a court ordered the Young LGBTI+ Association dissolved in December 2025. İzmir's proximity makes that ruling the most locally relevant judicial signal for a visitor based in Manisa.

Detention of trans people in Turkey is organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and LGBTI+ detainees are subject to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, with no policy or staff training to identify LGBTI+ needs. A trans visitor detained in Manisa would be held under that same national custody regime.

Foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' background checks, releasing them without fine but with names and details recorded.

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. These are national figures with no Manisa-specific breakdown in the sources.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the leaked 11th Judicial Package has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources; Human Rights Watch reported on it as a draft on 29 October 2025, and a February 2026 press report described a separate proposal not included in the 12th judicial package.

The sources contain no Manisa-specific statute, incident, police action or court decision. Enforcement patterns in pride bans, raids and detentions are documented for Istanbul, Ankara and İzmir, and cannot be assumed to map onto Manisa without local evidence.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking places Turkey 47th of 49, but the sources give no sub-national breakdown of how that score applies across provinces.

Whether the three draft law packages made public during 2025 will be resubmitted to parliament is not stated in the sources.
